title: The Wall Opens
subtitle: Warsaw, Beijing, Budapest, Leipzig, Berlin, Prague and Bucharest, 1989
intro: In 1989 the communist systems of Central and Eastern Europe came apart within a single year, and in China a protest movement was put down by force. This chapter sets side by side the people who wrote things down as it happened: a prime minister who lost an election, a premier who ordered troops into his capital (if the diary is his), the party chief who stood against him, the aide to the Soviet leader who refused to send tanks, the West German chancellor's adviser, an East German novelist, a dissident playwright, and the diplomats whose cables are now declassified.

The honest record here is mixed. True diaries exist and are published under their writers' names — Chernyaev, Rakowski, Teltschik, and the disputed text attributed to Li Peng — but much of what was written on the day was official: cables, a press conference transcript, speeches, a chronicle. Those are included with their form stated plainly. Garton Ash's essays are eyewitness reportage, not a diary. Copyright and privacy also shape the chapter: these are modern texts, so they are paraphrased rather than quoted, and only public figures and published authors appear.

Two days frame everything. On Sunday 4 June 1989 Poles voted in the first partly free election in the Soviet bloc, and Solidarity won almost every seat it could contest; on the same day, hours earlier by the clock, the army cleared central Beijing. On 9 November a Politburo spokesman misread a note at a press conference, and by midnight the Berlin Wall was open. Between them come Hungary's reburial of Imre Nagy and its opening of the Austrian border (the Pan-European Picnic of 19 August, for which no published diarist is included here), Leipzig's 9 October, and after them Prague's November and Romania's December.

Casualty figures for Beijing are contested and are reported here as each writer gave them. The Chinese government spoke of about 200–300 deaths including soldiers; foreign embassies and later researchers gave estimates from several hundred to several thousand; one British cable relayed a far higher figure. The chapter does not settle the question; it shows how differently it was seen from inside the Great Hall, from the diplomatic quarter, and from abroad.

Read together, the eyes show how much depended on decisions not taken: troops that did not fire in Leipzig, a Soviet leadership that did not intervene, an East German official who did not know what his own paper meant. They also show how quickly each writer's hopes were overtaken — Wolf's renewed socialism, Rakowski's reform communism, Chernyaev's faith in Gorbachev's pace.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Time zones matter on 4 June: Poland kept summer time (UTC+2) and China observed daylight saving time from 1986 to 1991, so Beijing was on UTC+9. The clearing of central Beijing in the small hours of 4 June therefore fell on the Saturday evening of 3 June in Warsaw, and the Polish polls opened at 6 a.m. — 1 p.m. in Beijing. Berlin and Prague were on Central European Time (UTC+1) in November; Schabowski's announcement came at about 18:53.

eyes.name: Mieczysław F. Rakowski
eyes.role: Prime Minister of the Polish People's Republic (from Sept 1988); from 29 July 1989 First Secretary of the ruling Polish United Workers' Party (PZPR)
eyes.vantage_label: head of the government that lost the vote
eyes.authenticity: Kept for decades and published under his own name as Dzienniki polityczne (10 vols, Iskry, 1998–2005); the volume for 1987–1990 covers the Round Table and the election. The 5 June 1989 entry is cited by Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (IPN).
eyes.bio: A journalist-turned-politician and long-time editor of the weekly Polityka, Rakowski was the reform-minded face of the regime that negotiated with Solidarity at the Round Table. His diary is the view from the losing side of the first semi-free election in the Soviet bloc: candid, rueful and self-justifying by turns.

sources.title: IPN Gdańsk historical supplement, 3–5 June 2022 (cites Rakowski's 5 June 1989 entry)
Dzieje.pl biography

eyes.name: Timothy Garton Ash
eyes.role: British historian and journalist, aged 33–34; reporting for The Spectator, The Independent and The New York Review of Books
eyes.side: Western observer, close to the opposition movements
eyes.authenticity: Eyewitness essays written within days or weeks of the events and collected in 1990 as We the People (UK) / The Magic Lantern (US); reissued 2014 and 2019. Reportage, not a diary; dates of his presence are given here as ranges where the book does not fix a day.
eyes.bio: Garton Ash had spent the 1980s writing about Solidarity and dissident Central Europe, and in 1989 he moved from capital to capital as the regimes fell. His chapters set Warsaw's ballot, Budapest's reburial of Imre Nagy, the opening of the Wall and the back rooms of Civic Forum side by side, which makes him the one eye in this chapter who sees almost the whole European sequence.

sources.title: The Magic Lantern (Atlantic Books edition page)

eyes.name: Li Peng
eyes.role: Premier of the People's Republic of China, member of the Politburo Standing Committee
eyes.where: Zhongnanhai and the Great Hall of the People, Beijing
eyes.authenticity: A manuscript titled The Critical Moment, presented as Li Peng's diary for 15 April–24 June 1989, reportedly prepared around 2004 and blocked by the leadership. New Century Press in Hong Kong announced it for June 2010 after concluding it 'should be authentic', then cancelled the Hong Kong release under pressure; copies later circulated abroad. Li Peng never publicly confirmed it. Treat every entry as disputed.
eyes.bio: Li Peng announced martial law in Beijing on 20 May 1989 and was the public face of the decision to clear the square. The diary attributed to him is the only purported day-by-day record from inside the Standing Committee, and it presents the crackdown as a necessary defence against 'turmoil' — the official view from the very centre.

sources.title: South China Morning Post: Li Peng's June 4 diary revelations
AsiaNews: Beijing blocks publication of the Li Peng diaries
Minjian archive record on the Li Peng diary

eyes.name: Zhao Ziyang
eyes.role: General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party, aged 69
eyes.vantage_label: party leader who opposed martial law
eyes.authenticity: His words to the hunger strikers before dawn on 19 May were broadcast and filmed, and the transcript is widely reproduced. His own reflections come from tapes recorded secretly under house arrest and published in 2009 as Prisoner of the State — a memoir written later.
eyes.bio: Zhao argued inside the leadership for dialogue with the students and against martial law, and lost. His visit to the square on 19 May was his last public appearance; he spent the remaining fifteen years of his life under house arrest. He is the counterweight to Li Peng: the same Standing Committee, the opposite conclusion.

sources.title: New Century Press / Prisoner of the State (via SCMP report on Bao Pu, publisher of Zhao's memoir)

eyes.name: US Embassy Beijing (situation reports)
eyes.role: The American embassy under Ambassador James Lilley, filing numbered situation reports ('SITREPs') to Washington
eyes.vantage_label: foreign diplomats in the same city
eyes.authenticity: Declassified and published by the National Security Archive (Electronic Briefing Book 16, 'Tiananmen Square, 1989: The Declassified History'). Cables were written in haste from embassy officers' observations and from contacts; they correct themselves over the following weeks.
eyes.bio: The embassy sent officers out into the streets and wrote up what they saw, hour by hour. Its reports run from wry accounts of unarmed soldiers turned back by crowds to the night of 3–4 June and, three weeks later, a careful attempt to reconstruct what had happened and where.

sources.title: National Security Archive: Tiananmen Square, 1989 — documents

eyes.name: Sir Alan Donald
eyes.role: British Ambassador to the People's Republic of China (1988–1991)
eyes.vantage_label: foreign ambassador in the same city
eyes.authenticity: Cable of 5 June 1989 held in the UK National Archives, released and first reported in December 2017. It relays information from a Chinese contact and was written within a day of the events.
eyes.bio: Donald's cable is one of the starkest diplomatic documents of June 1989, and one of the most debated. It records what he was told rather than what he saw, and its casualty figure is far higher than most later estimates — which is exactly why it belongs here, flagged.

sources.title: China Aerospace Studies Institute: UK cable on Tiananmen Square, June 4th 1989

eyes.name: Anatoly Chernyaev
eyes.role: Chief foreign-policy aide to Mikhail Gorbachev, aged 68
eyes.where: Moscow (the Kremlin and Central Committee); with Gorbachev in East Berlin, 6–7 October
eyes.vantage_label: inside the Soviet leadership, at a distance from the streets
eyes.authenticity: Kept nightly from the early 1970s; deposited at the Gorbachev Foundation and published in Russian. The 1989 volume was translated by Anna Melyakova and edited by Svetlana Savranskaya for the National Security Archive (EBB 275, 2009); individual entries also appear in the CEU Press documentary volume Masterpieces of History (2010).
eyes.bio: A veteran of the Second World War and a long-time Central Committee international official, Chernyaev became Gorbachev's closest adviser on foreign affairs. His diary is unusually frank: it records Gorbachev's private remarks, the aide's own impatience, and a sense — sharp by November — that he was watching the end of the order his generation had fought for.

sources.title: National Security Archive: The Diary of Anatoly Chernyaev, 1989 (EBB 275)
Excerpt, 10 November 1989 (National Security Archive)
Excerpt, 11 October 1989 (Making the History of 1989, RRCHNM)

eyes.name: Wolfgang Schneider (compiler)
eyes.role: Leipzig compiler and chronicler of the autumn demonstrations
eyes.authenticity: Leipziger Demontagebuch (Aufbau, Berlin, 1990): a dated chronicle of the Monday demonstrations with collected banners, chants and documents; its preface, 'Oktoberrevolution 1989', is a retrospective interpretation written in 1990. Excerpt translated by Jeremiah Riemer for German History in Documents and Images.
eyes.bio: Schneider's book gathered the slogans, leaflets and timings of Leipzig's autumn while they were still fresh. It is a chronicle rather than a diary, but its account of 9 October — the evening the state expected to use force and did not — is precise about times and numbers.

sources.title: GHDI: The Triumph of Nonviolence in Leipzig (October 9, 1989)

eyes.name: Christa Wolf
eyes.role: East German novelist, aged 60; SED member since 1949, a critical voice inside the system
eyes.form: dated speeches and appeals; annual diary
eyes.authenticity: Her Alexanderplatz speech of 4 November 1989 was broadcast live and printed; English translation in Jarausch and Gransow, Uniting Germany (1994), reproduced by GHDI. She also kept a diary of every 27 September from 1960 to 2000, published as Ein Tag im Jahr (2003; One Day a Year, 2007).
eyes.bio: Wolf was the GDR's most celebrated writer and one of those who hoped the autumn would produce a better socialism rather than the end of the state. Her speech on 4 November and her support for the 'For Our Country' appeal three weeks later record that hope at its height — and, read now, its brevity.

sources.title: GHDI: Speeches at the Alexanderplatz demonstration, 4 November 1989 (English PDF)
Complete Review: One Day a Year

eyes.name: Günter Schabowski
eyes.role: SED Politburo member and Berlin party chief, newly made the Politburo's spokesman, aged 60
eyes.where: International Press Centre, Mohrenstraße, East Berlin
eyes.vantage_label: official whose words opened the border
eyes.authenticity: Broadcast live on East German television; transcript published by Hans-Hermann Hertle and reproduced by the German federal government. Not a diary: an exact record of what was said in public, with times known to the minute.
eyes.bio: Schabowski had been handed the Council of Ministers' new travel regulation shortly before the press conference and had not been told it was meant to take effect the next day. His fumbled answer to a reporter's question is the most consequential slip of the tongue in the chapter.

sources.title: Bundesregierung: excerpt of the Schabowski press conference, 9 November 1989
Hertle, 'Sofort, unverzüglich' (bpb reading sample)

eyes.name: Horst Teltschik
eyes.role: Head of foreign and security policy in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office, aged 49
eyes.authenticity: Diary kept from 9 November 1989 to 3 October 1990; published as 329 Tage: Innenansichten der Einigung (Siedler, 1991) and in an expanded critical edition edited by Michael Gehler (Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 2024). Extracts translated by the Margaret Thatcher Foundation.
eyes.bio: Teltschik was Kohl's closest foreign-policy adviser and began his diary on the night the Wall opened, when he was with the chancellor on a state visit to Poland. His record is the West German government's view: phone calls with Washington, Paris, London and Moscow, and the drafting of the Ten-Point Plan.

sources.title: Margaret Thatcher Foundation: Teltschik diary, 10 November 1989 (translation)
Perlentaucher: Die 329 Tage zur deutschen Einigung (2024 edition)

eyes.name: Václav Havel
eyes.role: Playwright and dissident, co-founder of Charter 77, aged 53; leader of Civic Forum, then President of Czechoslovakia
eyes.vantage_label: opposition leader who became head of state
eyes.authenticity: Speeches recorded and printed at the time; the New Year's address of 1 January 1990 is published by the Czech presidential office in English translation. Not a diary.
eyes.bio: Havel had been in prison as recently as May 1989. Within six weeks of 17 November he went from the stage of the Laterna Magika theatre, where Civic Forum met, to Prague Castle. His speeches are the most articulate public statements of the year from a man who had spent it on the other side of power.

sources.title: World History Commons: Havel's New Year's Address to the Nation, 1990

eyes.name: Ion Bucur
eyes.role: Ambassador of the Socialist Republic of Romania to the USSR
eyes.authenticity: Cable to Bucharest dated 21 December 1989, translated by Mircea Munteanu for the Cold War International History Project. The Soviet Foreign Ministry's own memorandum of the same conversation survives and broadly matches it (Wilson Center Digital Archive).
eyes.bio: Bucur is the voice of the last hardline regime in the bloc, reporting to his capital on the day the regime was collapsing around it. That both sides' records of his meeting survive lets the reader hear one conversation from two ends.

sources.title: Making the History of 1989: The Possible Soviet Intervention in Romania (Bucur cable)
Wilson Center Digital Archive: Soviet memorandum of conversation with Ambassador I. Bucur, 21 Dec 1989

entries.headline: Premier writes that he is ready for the worst
entries.digest: In an entry from the early weeks of the protests that followed Hu Yaobang's death, the diary has Li Peng declare that he had braced for the worst from the start. He frames the student movement as 'turmoil' that could become a new Cultural Revolution, and presents himself as willing to sacrifice even his family's safety to prevent it.
entries.source_note: Paraphrased from the SCMP's summary of the manuscript (authenticity disputed).

entries.headline: At Deng's house, the decision for martial law
entries.digest: The diary describes a meeting at Deng Xiaoping's home with the Standing Committee and President Yang Shangkun, at which bringing troops into Beijing was agreed. It records Zhao Ziyang as the lone dissenter and Hu Qili as uneasy, and paints Zhao as crestfallen and Li himself as stirred. This is the leadership's own account of the turn from talk to force.
entries.source_note: SCMP summary of The Critical Moment, 17 May entry (disputed text).

entries.headline: Party chief tells hunger strikers he came too late
entries.digest: Before dawn Zhao went to the square with his aide Wen Jiabao, climbed into a bus of exhausted hunger strikers, and spoke to them through a megaphone. He told them, close to tears, that the leaders had come too late, that they should look after their health and end the fast, and that the problems could be solved over time. It was his last public appearance; martial law was declared the next day and he was soon removed.
entries.source_note: Widely reproduced broadcast transcript; context in Zhao's Prisoner of the State (2009).

entries.headline: Deng's instruction: minimise harm, but be prepared
entries.digest: The diary records Deng telling the leaders that troops enforcing martial law should try to avoid casualties but must be ready for them. The same day, it says, Jiang Zemin was chosen to replace Zhao as party leader, and Li gave his full support. Li announced martial law on television that night.
entries.source_note: SCMP summary of the 19 May entry (disputed text); martial law broadcast 19–20 May is well documented.

entries.headline: 'Martial law with Chinese characteristics': troops turned back
entries.digest: SITREP No. 27 describes lightly armed soldiers retreating in disarray from crowds who mocked them, an almost comic scene. Within hours SITREP No. 28 strikes a different note: some ten to fifteen thousand troops held at the city's edge, now in helmets and carrying automatic weapons, moving inward. The embassy concludes that force has become likely.
entries.source_note: NSA EBB 16, documents 10 and 11 (SITREPs 27 and 28, 3 June 1989).

entries.place: Great Hall of the People, Beijing
entries.headline: Meetings in the Great Hall as troops move in
entries.digest: According to the diary, Li spent the night in meetings in the Great Hall of the People about sending troops into the square, while Jiang Zemin watched from a nearby building. The text presents the night as an operation to restore order and is silent about what it cost the city around them.
entries.source_note: SCMP summary (disputed text).

entries.headline: The square is taken; the embassy counts the cost
entries.digest: SITREP No. 32, 'The Morning of June 4', reports that troops have taken the square and fired on demonstrators, and passes on reports of damage to shops and banks. A later cable that day notes tanks passing the diplomatic compound and gives first casualty figures, which the State Department's own task force that day put in a range from several hundred to over two thousand. The writers flag repeatedly that the numbers are uncertain.
entries.source_note: NSA EBB 16, documents 14–16.

entries.headline: Poland votes — and the vote is a rout
entries.digest: Garton Ash was in Warsaw for the first partly free election in the Soviet bloc, agreed at the Round Table: all Senate seats and a third of the Sejm open to contest. He describes Solidarity's candidates, each photographed beside Lech Wałęsa, sweeping the open seats, and voters crossing out the names on the government's 'national list'.
entries.source_note: The Magic Lantern / We the People, Warsaw chapter (publisher's description confirms 4 June presence).

entries.headline: The prime minister names it a day of defeat
entries.digest: With the first results in, Rakowski wrote in his diary that this was a day of great defeat for his side. He and his colleagues had expected the communist coalition to hold up; instead almost every contested seat went to Solidarity and most of the national list failed to reach the threshold. The IPN notes how uneasy the government's leaders looked that day.
entries.source_note: IPN Gdańsk historical supplement (June 2022), quoting Rakowski's 5 June 1989 entry.

entries.headline: A cable relays a casualty figure no one can check
entries.digest: Donald cabled London with an account he had received from a Chinese contact describing how the square and surrounding streets were cleared and putting the dead at a minimum of ten thousand. He reported it as information received, not as his own observation. The figure is far above the Chinese government's statement of about 200–300 dead and most later Western and independent estimates of several hundred to a few thousand; historians treat it as one contemporaneous claim among many.
entries.source_note: UK National Archives cable of 5 June 1989, released 2017; summarized by CASI.

entries.headline: Gunfire hits the diplomats' own compound
entries.digest: SITREP No. 38 reports that a passing army convoy fired into the diplomatic apartment compound where many foreign staff lived. The embassy speculates about motives, from nervous troops to a deliberate warning, and Washington begins to plan for evacuating dependants. Rumours of clashes between army units, reported the day before, are mostly refuted.
entries.source_note: NSA EBB 16, documents 21–22.

entries.headline: Budapest reburies Imre Nagy
entries.digest: Twelve days after the Polish vote, Garton Ash stood in Heroes' Square for the ceremonial reburial of Imre Nagy, the reform communist executed after the 1956 uprising. He describes the coffins, the crowds, and speeches by young opposition figures that would have been unthinkable a year earlier. To him the ceremony was the moment Hungary's regime publicly conceded its founding lie.
entries.source_note: The Magic Lantern, Budapest chapter; date of reburial is well established.

entries.headline: Three weeks on: 'What happened on the night of June 3/4?'
entries.digest: With time to sift reports, the embassy produced a reconstruction with a timeline. It concluded that most of the killing happened on the avenues leading to the square rather than in the square itself, and that civilian deaths were probably below three thousand. It is the cautious, revised voice of the same observers who had written in haste on 4 June.
entries.source_note: NSA EBB 16, document 31 (embassy cable, 22 June 1989).

entries.headline: On the eve of the GDR's fortieth birthday
entries.digest: As Gorbachev prepared to fly to East Berlin for the GDR's fortieth anniversary celebrations, Chernyaev noted his chief's reluctance to go and his determination not to lend Honecker his support. Tens of thousands of East Germans had already left through Hungary and the embassies in Prague and Warsaw. The aide expected the trip to be awkward rather than historic.
entries.source_note: Chernyaev diary, 5 Oct 1989 (Masterpieces of History, doc. 87; content paraphrased from secondary summaries).

entries.place: Leipzig city centre and ring road
entries.headline: Leipzig: the evening force was expected and did not come
entries.digest: Schneider sets out the state's preparations: factory workers warned to stay out of the centre after four, parents told to fetch children early, some three thousand police plus factory militias and Stasi units deployed. About seventy thousand people gathered after the prayers for peace at St Nicholas and other churches. An appeal for calm from six local figures, including conductor Kurt Masur and three SED district secretaries, was read in the churches and broadcast at six; by about 6:25 the armed units were pulling back. He credits the crowd's persistence more than the appeal.
entries.source_note: Leipziger Demontagebuch (1990), preface; GHDI translation.

entries.headline: Reading the transcript of Gorbachev and Honecker
entries.digest: Back in Moscow, Chernyaev read the record of Gorbachev's Berlin talks and noted his chief's contemptuous private verdict on Honecker. Gorbachev thought the old man could have bowed out with dignity, citing age and health. Chernyaev and Shakhnazarov doubted even that would have saved his reputation, which, he wrote, his own people had already cursed. He noted that the SED Politburo was in its second day of session and that Egon Krenz seemed to be moving.
entries.source_note: Chernyaev diary, 11 Oct 1989 (Making the History of 1989, item 423).

entries.headline: Christa Wolf asks the crowd to dream — with their eyes open
entries.digest: Speaking to the largest demonstration in GDR history, Wolf said the revolution had first freed language itself: stiff official German was giving way to living speech. She disliked the regime's word 'Wende', preferring 'revolutionary renewal' from below, and asked people to imagine a socialism no one would want to flee. She warned against officials changing sides too nimbly and called 'We are the people' the most important sentence of the autumn.
entries.source_note: GHDI, speeches at Alexanderplatz, 4 Nov 1989 (trans. Jarausch and Gransow).

entries.headline: 'As far as I know — immediately'
entries.digest: Near the end of a long, dull press conference, Schabowski read out a new regulation allowing private travel abroad and permanent exit through any border crossing, including into West Berlin. A journalist asked when it took effect. Shuffling his papers, Schabowski said that as far as he knew it applied at once, without delay; asked about passports, he said that was a technical question. He had not been told the rule was meant to start the next morning. Within hours crowds were at the checkpoints.
entries.source_note: Transcript excerpt (Hertle, Die Berliner Mauer, 2009), Bundesregierung.

entries.headline: News reaches the chancellor's party in Poland
entries.digest: Teltschik's diary opens on the night Chancellor Kohl, on a long-planned state visit to Poland, learned that East Berlin's border was opening. The first reports by telephone from Bonn were confused, and Kohl at first doubted them. The question that dominated the night was whether the chancellor could break off a visit meant to reconcile Germans and Poles.
entries.source_note: 329 Tage (1991), opening entry; corroborated by Stephan Eisel's account of the Bonn end of the same evening.

entries.headline: Breaking off the Poland visit
entries.digest: Kohl decided to interrupt the visit and called an emergency cabinet meeting, intending to telephone Bush, Mitterrand, Thatcher and Gorbachev at once. West German planes could not fly through East German airspace into Berlin, so the party flew round via Sweden to Hamburg and switched to an American military aircraft. That evening Kohl spoke at a rally outside Schöneberg town hall, where part of the crowd whistled him down. Teltschik also noted Thatcher's public welcome of the day.
entries.source_note: Teltschik diary, 10 Nov 1989 (Thatcher Foundation translation); route from Eisel, Helmut Kohl – Nahaufnahme (2010).

entries.headline: 'The Berlin Wall has collapsed'
entries.digest: Chernyaev wrote that the Wall had fallen and with it an entire era of the socialist system. He listed the leaders already gone that autumn and the few left — Castro, Ceaușescu, Kim Il Sung — whom he saw as hostile to Moscow anyway. He called it the end of Yalta and of the Stalinist legacy, a change in the world balance of power, and credited Gorbachev with letting history take its natural course.
entries.source_note: National Security Archive excerpt, 10 Nov 1989 (trans. Vladislav Zubok); NPR, 8 Nov 2009.

entries.headline: At the Wall in the first days
entries.digest: Garton Ash describes the first days after the opening: East Berliners queuing at the checkpoints, then walking into the West to look, shop with their welcome money, and go home again. What struck him was the ordinariness — families, Trabants, people who mostly returned the same night. He read it as the people of East Germany taking back a right rather than fleeing.
entries.source_note: The Magic Lantern, Berlin chapter; exact days of his presence not fixed here.

entries.headline: Away from Prague on the night it began
entries.digest: Havel was at his country house when a sanctioned student march in Prague, marking fifty years since the Nazi closure of Czech universities, was halted and beaten by riot police on Národní třída. Rumours spread that a student had been killed (it proved false). He returned to Prague the next day to a city in uproar.
entries.source_note: Standard chronologies of 17–18 November 1989; not a diary entry.

entries.headline: Civic Forum is founded
entries.digest: At a meeting in the Drama Club theatre, Havel and other opposition figures founded Civic Forum, demanding the resignation of those responsible for the 1968 invasion and for the police violence, and the release of political prisoners. Students and theatres had already declared strikes. Civic Forum soon moved its headquarters to the Laterna Magika theatre.
entries.source_note: Standard chronologies; date of founding well established.

entries.headline: Havel speaks from the balcony
entries.digest: From the balcony of the Melantrich publishing house above Wenceslas Square, Havel addressed a crowd of some two hundred thousand. He called for dialogue, nonviolence and a general strike, and read Civic Forum's demands. Many in the square had never heard him speak in public; his writings had circulated only in samizdat.
entries.source_note: Standard chronologies; crowd figure approximate.

entries.headline: In the back rooms of Civic Forum
entries.digest: Garton Ash spent days in the dressing rooms and corridors of the Laterna Magika, where Civic Forum improvised a revolution between rehearsal spaces, typewriters and constant press conferences. He describes Havel as a stage manager of events, and the general strike of 27 November as the moment the workers' state found its workers against it. His famous line that what took Poland ten years took East Germany ten weeks and might take Czechoslovakia ten days dates from this visit.
entries.source_note: The Magic Lantern, Prague chapter (publisher's description confirms Laterna Magika); dates given as a range.

entries.headline: The Ten-Point Plan goes to the Bundestag
entries.digest: Teltschik records that Kohl presented a Ten-Point Plan for overcoming the division of Germany and Europe, drafted in a small circle in the chancellery and kept from coalition partners and allies until the speech. The plan sketched confederative structures leading in time to a federation. Teltschik's diary is frank that domestic politics shaped the timing.
entries.source_note: 329 Tage, entry of 28 Nov 1989; Perlentaucher review summary of the 2024 edition.

entries.headline: 'For Our Country': an appeal to keep the GDR
entries.digest: Wolf was among the first signatories of the appeal 'Für unser Land', read to the press by the writer Stefan Heym on 28 November. It asked East Germans to choose an independent, democratic and socialist GDR rather than be absorbed by the Federal Republic. Within weeks the appeal had many signatures, including those of Egon Krenz and other SED leaders, which harmed it with many; the Leipzig crowds were by then chanting for unity.
entries.source_note: Well-documented appeal; Wolf's role from standard biographies.

entries.headline: Romania's ambassador and a Soviet minister talk past each other
entries.digest: Bucur handed Deputy Foreign Minister Ivan Aboimov the text of Ceaușescu's 20 December speech, which blamed the unrest in Timișoara on plots by Warsaw Pact states. Aboimov asked about deaths in Timișoara; Bucur said he had no information. The Soviet side rejected the accusations as groundless and repeated its line of non-interference. That same day in Bucharest, Ceaușescu's mass rally broke up in jeers; the next day he fled the capital.
entries.source_note: Bucur cable (CWIHP / Making the History of 1989, item 204); Soviet memcon, Wilson Center doc. 111562.

entries.headline: The dissident becomes president
entries.digest: The Federal Assembly, still largely composed of deputies elected under the old regime, unanimously elected Havel President of Czechoslovakia; Alexander Dubček had been chosen to chair the Assembly the day before. Six months earlier Havel had been a prisoner on parole.
entries.source_note: Well-established date of the presidential election.

entries.headline: A year-end letter to Gorbachev
entries.digest: Chernyaev closed his 1989 diary not with an entry but with a letter to Gorbachev setting out his disappointments: indecision on economic reform, on land and on the nationalities. The year that ended the Soviet bloc in Europe left Gorbachev's own aide uneasy about the Soviet Union itself.
entries.source_note: National Security Archive EBB 275 description of the final entry.

entries.headline: New Year: 'our country is not flourishing'
entries.digest: In his first address as president Havel told listeners that he would not lie to them: the economy was wasteful, the land among the most polluted in Europe, life expectancy low. Worse, he said, was a contaminated moral environment, in which everyone had learned to say one thing and think another, and all shared some responsibility. He announced a broad amnesty and ended by telling the people that their government had returned to them.
entries.source_note: Presidential office translation via World History Commons.

convergences.label: Tiananmen and the Polish election on the same day
convergences.note: In Beijing the embassy counts casualties and the Li Peng diary speaks of restoring order; in Warsaw Garton Ash watches ballots and Rakowski, next morning, writes of defeat. Two communist governments faced their societies on the same day and chose opposite answers.

convergences.label: Martial law decided; Zhao goes to the square
convergences.note: Two members of the same Standing Committee on the same day: one telling the hunger strikers that the leaders came too late, the other recording the instruction to prepare troops.

convergences.label: Leipzig's Monday demonstration
convergences.note: Schneider records the streets; two days later Chernyaev reads the transcript of Gorbachev and Honecker in Moscow. The decision not to shoot in Leipzig was local, but Moscow's refusal to back Honecker was its backdrop.

convergences.label: The Wall opens
convergences.note: An East German official's slip, a West German chancellor stranded in Warsaw, a Soviet aide calling it the end of an era, a British reporter at the crossings — and a novelist who five days earlier had asked for a socialism nobody would want to leave.

convergences.label: Two plans for Germany on one day
convergences.note: Kohl's Ten-Point Plan for a path to German unity and the 'For Our Country' appeal for an independent GDR were made public on the same Tuesday.

convergences.label: Prague's November
convergences.note: Havel's public words and Garton Ash's view from the back rooms of the same theatre.

convergences.label: Romania's last days under Ceaușescu
convergences.note: Bucur relays his capital's accusations to a Soviet ministry that rejects them; Chernyaev, on 10 November, had already counted Ceaușescu among the last holdouts.

ties.note: Both sat on the Politburo Standing Committee; Zhao opposed martial law, Li announced it and succeeded in having Zhao removed.
As Polish party leader, Rakowski was among the bloc leaders at the GDR's fortieth-anniversary celebrations in East Berlin on 6–7 October 1989, where Chernyaev accompanied Gorbachev.
The two leaders' foreign-policy aides worked opposite each other through 1990 on the terms of German unification.
Garton Ash worked alongside Civic Forum at the Laterna Magika and knew Havel from the dissident years.
Both spoke at the Alexanderplatz demonstration of 4 November 1989, Schabowski as the SED's representative, to a hostile reception.
Garton Ash wrote as a sympathiser of Solidarity, whose victory Rakowski recorded as a defeat.
Both missions were in Beijing's Jianguomenwai diplomatic quarter and reported the same nights, with very different casualty figures.

threads_out.note: Chernyaev wrote on 10 November that the Wall's fall ended the Stalinist legacy. In the same year the Soviet state was formally rehabilitating victims of the 1930s purges, and the Memorial society was gathering their names.
Chernyaev called 9 November the end of the Yalta order. The division of Germany and of Europe that ended in 1989 was the settlement of 1945, and Chernyaev himself had fought in that war.
Chernyaev saw November 1989 as the end of an era for the socialist system that 1917 had begun; two years later the Soviet Union itself was gone.

The space race of the 1960s was one of the Cold War's contests. At Malta in December 1989 Bush and Gorbachev held a summit widely seen as marking the end of that rivalry, twenty years after Apollo 11.

Several of these diaries survived because institutions took them in: Chernyaev's at the Gorbachev Foundation and in the National Security Archive's translations, and Teltschik's in a critical edition 35 years on. The declassified cables are now part of the same archive of many eyes.
